proposals.name: Deadpan normalization of an extreme or impossible situation
proposals.instruction: Score how completely the speaker treats an evidently extraordinary predicament as routine, with no astonishment, no comment on the strangeness, and no raised voice. 10 = the line is delivered in the flat register of ordinary problem-solving or mild inconvenience while the situation it presupposes is plainly catastrophic, surreal, or life-altering ('let's just take the stairs'; 'it's only until we board the plane'). 5 = the speaker is calm but still explicitly registers that something is odd. 0 = the line is openly astonished, alarmed, or exclamatory about its own situation, or contains no implied situation at all.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side is dominated by unruffled, procedural-sounding lines whose comedy is entirely in the mismatch between tone and stakes: R01 ('no idea, let's just take the stairs'), R19 ('this is so much easier. i wish i thought of it sooner'), R30 ('it's only until we board the plane'), R53 ('if this doesn't break our lease, i don't have any better ideas'). A criterion bank built on visible joke features has nothing to grip here, because the line's surface is deliberately featureless. R20 and R48 are the same move in corporate/IT register.

proposals.name: Enters mid-conversation, presupposing an unseen prior turn
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the caption reads as the second or later turn of an already-running exchange, so that a whole prior utterance and relationship must be inferred. 10 = the line is only interpretable by reconstructing what was said to the speaker a moment earlier, and that reconstruction is itself the joke ('about three years. how long have you been here'; 'no, i can't help you get out of it like always'). 5 = some conversational framing but the line stands alone fine. 0 = a standalone announcement, label, or opening remark that presupposes nothing prior.
proposals.rationale: R42 answers an unheard question and volleys it back; R37 ('we're just having game night. what about you') and R22 ('did i miss anything') and R47 ('did we forget anything') all import an entire unstated exchange; R27's doubled 'no...and no...' implies years of prior asking. R04 ('but you must have seen her!') is a rebuttal to an unheard denial. All are dense-high with very low card scores, suggesting the scorecard scores only what is written and cannot credit the implied turn.

proposals.name: Speaker self-indictment: character exposed rather than scene described
proposals.instruction: Score how much the line reveals about the speaker's character, blindness, or vanity as opposed to reporting on the world. 10 = the speaker damns, exposes, or diminishes themself without realizing it, or with rueful awareness, and the reader learns who this person is ('at least i know i'm a puppet'; 'this is why nobody likes to play with you'; 'do you have any idea who you're talking to'). 5 = mild personality is visible but the line is mostly informational. 0 = the speaker is a neutral narrator with no exposed self-interest, ego, or blind spot.
proposals.rationale: R11, R10, R45, R58 ('does this make me look middle aged') and R51 ('what if i don't identify with either') are all dense-high with card percentiles under .25. Each supplies a character rather than a gag; a bank of joke-craft criteria measures wordplay and topicality and would find nothing to score in a bare, unfunny-on-its-face confession of vanity or self-pity.

proposals.name: Adds an unseen frame rather than annotating what is depicted
proposals.instruction: Score how much new, non-obvious situation the caption supplies beyond naming or reacting to the evident content of the scene. 10 = the line introduces a wholly new premise, relationship, or offstage world that could not be read off the picture. 5 = partly new, partly a restatement. 0 = the caption is essentially a caption in the descriptive sense: it identifies or comments on the visible situation ('wow, i guess venice really is sinking'; 'so, you're a fixture at this spot huh'; 'we're dinosaurs, ronny'), telling the reader what they can already see.
proposals.rationale: R06, R18, R34, and R33 ('roaming charges? seriously') sit at dense percentiles .10-.21 while the scorecard puts them at .86-.98. These lines are well-formed, on-topic, and neatly matched to their scene, which is exactly what an explicit criterion for relevance or fit would reward; but they add nothing the reader did not already have, which is likely what the dense model penalizes.

proposals.name: Joke not fully resolved by a self-contained pun
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the line's humor survives independently of a single pun or double meaning that closes inside the text. 10 = no pivot word carries the joke; the comedy comes from stance, situation, or implication. 5 = there is wordplay but the line would still work without it. 0 = the entire line exists to deliver one double-sense term and dies once that term is decoded ('special tonight - spare ribs'; 'stairway to heaven, guys, the short version'; 'you've been selected for downsizing, too'; 'watch me pull out some hidden fees from thin air').
proposals.rationale: R49, R13, R08, and R54 are all dense-low (.06-.16) and card-high (.76-.96). A criterion bank almost certainly contains an explicit wordplay/cleverness item, and these maximize it: the pun is legible, well-executed, and confirmable from the text. The dense model appears to treat a fully-resolving pun as a terminal joke with no residue, which is the opposite of how the bank scores it.

proposals.name: Withholds the gloss; no clause explaining its own joke
proposals.instruction: Score how far the line trusts the reader to complete it. 10 = the mechanism is never named; the line stops at the point of maximum inference. 5 = one small helping phrase. 0 = the caption states its premise and then appends an explanatory clause, apposition, or qualifier that spells out why it is funny ('it's the trump lure -- it works best with bottom feeders'; '...but you're not going to escape your fossil fuel destiny'; 'stairway to heaven, guys, the short version').
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense .198 / card .993) and R26 (dense .021 / card .732) both name the device and then explain it, and R13 tags its reference then qualifies it. The explanatory clause adds scoreable, checkable content -- a judge reading a criterion about clarity or setup-payoff structure sees a complete, well-formed joke -- while the dense model appears to read the gloss as a deflation.

proposals.name: Independence from a named topical figure or news-cycle referent
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the humor survives if every proper noun tied to a current news figure, politician, or product-of-the-moment is removed. 10 = no such reference, or the reference is incidental. 5 = a topical name is present but the underlying joke stands on its own. 0 = a named political figure or news-cycle item is the punchline itself, so that the line has no content once the name is stripped ('they've come back for marjorie taylor greene'; 'perhaps elon musk does have too much money'; 'if trump wins again, go ahead and close up this window').
proposals.rationale: R40, R56, R39, R23, R15 and R36 are all dense-low (.02-.23) and card-high (.73-.99). Topicality and cultural reference are natural, easily-written criteria and these items maximize them; the dense model appears to discount reference-as-punchline, treating the named figure as borrowed rather than earned laughter. R57's 'no fox news' is dense-high, but there the reference is a throwaway rider on a situation, not the payload.

proposals.name: Free of stance markers that instruct the reader to be amused
proposals.instruction: Score the absence of framing tokens that pre-announce the line as a joke or pre-license the reader's reaction: 'wow', 'seriously', 'can you believe', 'you think that's bad', 'i guess', 'perhaps', 'huh'. 10 = a plain declarative or plain question with no reaction-cueing scaffolding. 5 = one mild marker. 0 = the line opens or closes with an explicit reaction cue doing the comedic lifting ('wow, i guess venice really is sinking'; 'roaming charges? seriously'; 'can you believe that this was easier to get...'; 'you think that's bad, my husband is...').
proposals.rationale: R06, R33, R41 and R46 are dense .004-.226 against card .92-.94. The markers make the intended reading explicit and therefore highly legible to any criterion about clarity of comedic intent, but they also do the reader's reacting for them. By contrast the dense-high lines R01, R22, R31, R42 carry no such scaffolding at all.

proposals.name: Brevity carrying implied backstory, not brevity as bare label
proposals.instruction: Composite. First judge how short the line is, then judge how much unstated situation it obliges the reader to construct; score the conjunction. 10 = very few words that nonetheless imply a full offstage history, relationship, or preceding catastrophe ('did i miss anything'; 'did we forget anything'; 'try not to overthink it'). 5 = short with modest implication, or long with rich implication. 0 = short and inert -- a bare label, menu item, or two-way choice that implies nothing beyond itself ('chicken or rabbit'), or long and still implying nothing.
proposals.rationale: This composite is needed because length alone splits both ways in the slice. R22 (4 words, dense .907) and R47 (3 words, dense .868) and R31 (5 words, dense .887) are terse and dense-high; R24 ('chicken or rabbit', 3 words, dense .013, card .874) is equally terse and dense-low. A criterion bank scoring concision or economy would rank all four alike; the separating variable is implied world per word, not word count.

proposals.name: Restraint from numeric or inventory specificity substituting for wit
proposals.instruction: Score the absence of precise quantities, enumerated lists, times, or dollar figures that supply an appearance of comic craft without an actual turn. 10 = no such specificity, or a deliberately vague quantity ('about three years'). 5 = one number that genuinely carries the joke. 0 = the line is built around counted items, exact figures, or a countdown ('four hot dogs, 2 boxes of cracker jack and 2 sheets of drywall'; 'a delay between one and ten hours'; 'lost 45 pounds'; 'his full 1200 stimulus'; 'if you are not back by 11 30').
proposals.rationale: R12, R07, R25, R36 and R52 are dense .06-.19 and card .76-.98. Specific detail is a classic writing virtue and an easy criterion to write and verify, so it is likely over-credited; the dense model seems to read enumerated precision as padding. Note R42's 'about three years' deliberately blurs its number and is dense .968.

proposals.name: Question whose presupposition is the joke
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line is a question (or request) that quietly presupposes an absurd state of affairs as settled and unremarkable. 10 = a mundane, sincerely-asked question whose presupposition is what detonates ('did i miss anything'; 'what if i don't identify with either'; 'does this make me look middle aged'; 'can i get a discount? this fish is dead'). 5 = a question that is merely rhetorical or a setup line. 0 = not a question, or a question whose presupposition is entirely ordinary.
proposals.rationale: R22, R47, R51, R58, R32 and R45 are all dense-high (.82-.97) with card percentiles .10-.23. The interrogative form gives these lines no visible punchline at all -- syntactically they are requests for information -- so an explicitly-written bank looking for a setup and a payoff will find only a setup. What carries them is the presupposition, which is never stated.

proposals.name: Institutional or domestic register transplanted intact into an impossible setting
proposals.instruction: Score how exactly the line reproduces the unaltered idiom of a mundane institution -- HR, IT support, tenancy, remote work, retail, auto repair -- while the situation it addresses is manifestly not one of those. 10 = a verbatim-sounding piece of workplace or household boilerplate with no comic embellishment, deployed where it cannot possibly apply ('you now report directly to me'; 'have you tried unplugging it'; 'maybe we should go back to working remotely'; 'if this doesn't break our lease'). 5 = register borrowed but visibly played with. 0 = no borrowed institutional register, or the register is announced and parodied rather than delivered straight.
proposals.rationale: R38, R48, R20, R53 and R03 ('well, there's your problem, we'll need to change attire', mechanic's idiom) are dense .82-.97, card .04-.24. The comedy is a register collision that leaves no lexical trace of a joke -- every word is dull by design. Contrast R17, which parodies an airline-announcement register loudly and self-consciously and lands at dense .110 / card .934: the bank rewards visible register play, the dense model rewards the invisible kind.

proposals.name: Sayable as speech, not written-to-be-read prose
proposals.instruction: Score whether the line is something a person would plausibly say aloud, in this tone, in this moment. 10 = idiomatic spoken English with natural rhythm, contractions, and the imprecision of real speech. 5 = plausible but slightly composed. 0 = literary or stilted construction that betrays an author writing for a reader ('you flit home reeking of pollen and nectar'; 'so litigation continues to exist in advanced civilizations'), including announcer or narrator voices delivered as set pieces.
proposals.rationale: R44 (dense .106 / card .830), R59 (dense .101 / card .969) and R17 (dense .110 / card .934) are all crafted, decorative, or performative prose. Craft-shaped criteria -- vividness, imagery, elevated diction -- reward exactly this. Meanwhile the dense-high lines R01, R31, R37, R42 are conversationally flat to the point of plainness. This is a distinct axis from A01: a line can be deadpan yet still written rather than spoken.

proposals.name: Discomfort carried by indirection rather than stated shock
proposals.instruction: Score how a transgressive, taboo, or painful element is handled. 10 = the edge is real but arrives obliquely, through euphemism, understatement, or a sideways admission the reader must complete ('i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince'; 'to begin with, i am not anti-vacs'; 'what if i don't identify with either'). 5 = an edge stated plainly without either shock or indirection. 0 = the discomfiting content is stated flatly for its shock value and the shock is the whole payload ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg'; 'another job lost to illegal aliens').
proposals.rationale: R02 (dense .753 / card .045), R29 (dense .938 / card .203) and R51 (dense .896 / card .148) all approach sensitive ground sidelong and score low on the card. R25 (dense .133 / card .975), R15 (dense .216 / card .986) and R36 (dense .021 / card .881) state the shocking thing outright and score very high on the card. This suggests a bank criterion that registers presence of edge or boldness without distinguishing earned indirection from blunt statement.

proposals.name: Cliche torqued one notch past its ordinary use
proposals.instruction: Score whether a familiar idiom, script, or stock phrase is taken and pushed one step further into a new claim rather than merely deployed. 10 = the received phrase is extended, inverted, or given a second clause that turns it into an original observation ('have you tried unplugging it and leaving it unplugged'; 'everyone ignores the elephant in the room, but take one on the elevator and everyone has something to say'). 5 = a cliche used aptly and unchanged. 0 = a stock phrase, song title, or standard gag script dropped in unmodified as if the recognition itself were the joke ('stairway to heaven, guys'; 'okay on three yank on the table cloth').
proposals.rationale: R48 (dense .966) and R60 (dense .727, card .001) both take a worn phrase and add the extra turn; R03's 'well, there's your problem' redirects a mechanic's cliche onto attire, and R31's 'try not to overthink it' inverts advice into an accusation. Against these, R13 (dense .062 / card .779) and R28 (dense .047 / card .833) invoke a recognizable script and stop. Recognition is easy to score explicitly; the extra torque is not, which is a plausible source of the split.

proposals.name: Textual bulk: word count and clause count
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the sheer textual bulk of the caption, counting words and independent/subordinate clauses only. 0 = a bare fragment of one to four words with at most one predicate; 3 = a short single clause of about five to eight words; 5 = one full sentence of roughly nine to thirteen words; 8 = two sentences or one sentence with a subordinate clause, roughly fourteen to twenty words; 10 = more than twenty words spanning two or more coordinated or subordinated clauses. Count only. Do not consider whether the length suits the caption, whether the caption is funny, clever, well-paced or effective, and do not treat brevity or elaboration as a virtue in either direction.
proposals.rationale: Length is a classic verbosity proxy that any rubric-aggregating scorer can accumulate credit on (more words = more criteria with something to grab) while a holistic reader may not. The slice spans nearly an order of magnitude in bulk: R39 (25 words, two coordinated clauses) and R47 (28 words with a conditional clause) sit at opposite ends of the disagreement from R05 ('chicken or rabbit', 3 words) and R59 ('did we forget anything', 4 words). R04 and R57 are likewise long, R30 and R25 near-minimal. Bulk is not the same thing as being a good contest entry, so it must be declared a nuisance rather than admitted to the bank.

proposals.name: Orthographic irregularities from entry form and normalization
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many surface orthographic irregularities are visible in the caption string, relative to conventional edited prose. Count instances of: a missing apostrophe in a contraction or possessive; a numeral written as digits where the surrounding text spells numbers as words (or the reverse) inside the same caption; internal punctuation that appears stripped, spaced out, or replaced by a space (e.g. a time or abbreviation split across a space); letter-by-letter period abbreviations; missing or absent terminal punctuation where a full sentence has been completed; unmatched or improvised quotation marks. 0 = none of these; 5 = one clear instance; 10 = three or more distinct instances. Report the count of visible irregularities only. Do not judge whether the irregularities are sloppy, charming, deliberate, or damaging, and do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: entries typed on a phone into a web form, and then passed through a lowercasing/punctuation-stripping normalization step, leave a residue that has nothing to do with the joke. The fingerprint is visible: R60 writes 'its hard to decide' with no apostrophe, R47 renders a clock time as '11 30' with the colon gone, R56 renders 'o.b.g.y.n' letter-by-letter, and R08 mixes a spelled 'four hot dogs' with digit '2 boxes' in one breath. A text-only model can key on this residue; it is a channel about the submission apparatus, not about the entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission device and entry-form / corpus text-normalization pipeline

proposals.name: Named political figures and partisan-aligned targets
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption names or unmistakably points at a real political figure, party, partisan media outlet, or partisan-coded public individual. 0 = no reference to any real political or public figure or outlet; 4 = an oblique or generic political reference with no named target; 7 = one named real political figure, outlet, or partisan-coded public individual; 10 = a named target that is also the pivot of the whole caption, or more than one such named target. Score presence and prominence of the named target only. Do not judge whether the political reference is apt, funny, fair, tired, or agreeable, do not judge your own or anyone's agreement with its stance, and do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: submitters to this venue know the readership's political lean and can farm agreement rather than laughs; a scorer trained or written against such a corpus can inherit the reward for the in-group jab. The fingerprint is the named target itself: R12 ('if trump wins again'), R18 ('marjorie taylor greene'), R31 ('the trump lure'), R40 ('no fox news'), R50 ('perhaps elon musk does have too much money'). Agreement-with-the-target is not how good the caption is, so this belongs in the discount set.
proposals.upstream_parent: alignment between the submitter's politics and the venue readership's politics (audience flattery)

proposals.name: Scene-anchored concrete object nouns
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption names concrete, physical, picturable objects, settings, or props rather than speaking only in abstractions or pronouns. 0 = no concrete noun at all; the caption is pronouns, generic nouns ('anything', 'it', 'this'), and verbs; 5 = one concrete picturable noun; 8 = two or more concrete picturable nouns; 10 = three or more, or one unusual and highly specific object named as the caption's hinge. Count only the presence and specificity of physical nouns. Do not judge whether the named object fits any drawing, whether the anchoring is skillful, or whether the caption is funny or good.
proposals.rationale: A criterion bank almost certainly contains something like 'engages the specifics of the scene', and explicit object nouns are the cheapest way to trip it. The slice splits sharply on this: R08 ('drywall', 'hot dogs', 'cracker jack'), R34 ('chandelier'), R36 ('table cloth'), and R47 ('screen door') carry heavy object vocabulary, while R30 ('did i miss anything'), R59 ('did we forget anything'), R48 ('try not to overthink it') and R16 carry none at all. Tagged mixed because genuine engagement with a drawing can also produce concrete nouns, so the discount must be reported as a sensitivity band rather than applied unconditionally.

proposals.name: Mid-conversation opener with unresolved anaphora
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is written as a continuation of speech already in progress rather than as a self-contained utterance. Award points for: a sentence-initial discourse connective or concessive ('well,', 'at least', 'to begin with', 'so,', 'but', 'and', 'i guess', 'i suppose', 'no idea,', 'okay'); a pronoun, demonstrative, or definite description with no antecedent inside the caption ('this', 'that', 'it', 'him', 'either', 'one'); an answer supplied to a question that is not shown; a second-person reference to a prior claim. 0 = fully self-contained, every referent introduced in the text; 5 = one such device; 10 = an opener that is both connective-initial and dependent on two or more unshown referents. Score the syntactic dependence only. Do not judge whether the in-progress framing works, whether it reads naturally, or whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: This is a stylistic register (the overheard-fragment voice) rather than a property of the joke, and the two scorers plainly weight it differently. R06 ('at least i know i'm a puppet'), R51 ('well, there's your problem'), R14 ('to begin with, i am not anti-vacs'), R28 ('no idea, let's just take the stairs'), R41 ('it's only until we board the plane') and R58 ('about three years. how long have you been here') all open mid-stream and all sit in the dense-high / card-low half. A scorecard written for standalone readability will systematically penalize the register itself, which is not a quality difference.

proposals.name: Perishable news-cycle and pandemic-era markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption depends on a topical circumstance with a short shelf life, i.e. a fact, policy, product, or condition that was salient for a bounded stretch of time and would need explaining to a reader outside that window. Examples of the kind of marker to count: a named relief payment or benefit amount, a named piece of protective or medical equipment tied to an emergency, a named ongoing election or campaign event, shifts in work arrangements tied to an emergency, a named epidemiological controversy. 0 = the caption's premise is time-independent; 5 = one dateable topical marker that colors but does not carry the caption; 10 = the caption's entire premise collapses without the dated circumstance. Score datedness only. Do not judge whether the topicality is fresh, stale, apt, or lazy, and do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: when an entry was submitted determines what was in the air, and different weeks draw different crowd sizes and different crowd moods; none of that is a property of the entry's merit. The fingerprint is explicit in the text: R46 ('his full 1200 stimulus'), R49 ('easier to get than an n95 mask'), R37 ('go back to working remotely'), R14 ('i am not anti-vacs'), and R12 ('if trump wins again'). Scoring the visible datedness lets us discount the timing effect without ever needing the unobservable submission date.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing (which contest week / which news window the entry was written in)

proposals.name: Recycled idiom, catchphrase or borrowed title template
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption is built on a pre-existing fixed phrase rather than on freshly assembled wording. Count: a stock idiom or proverb used whole or with one substitution; a well-known song, film, or book title; a recognizable service-script or announcement formula (airline PA, tech-support line, menu board, magician's patter, retail script); a familiar joke frame. 0 = no recognizable pre-existing phrase; 5 = one stock phrase present but subordinate; 8 = the stock phrase is the caption's spine; 10 = the caption is essentially the stock phrase with a single word swapped. Score recognizability and structural load of the borrowed phrase only. Do not judge whether the borrowing is clever, hackneyed, well-twisted, or effective, and do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: people who submit week after week absorb a shared inventory of frames from previously published winners, and reusing an inventory frame is a community-membership signal, not a merit signal. The fingerprint is the frame itself: R39 leans on 'the elephant in the room', R11 on a song title ('stairway to heaven'), R13 on the magician's 'pull ... out of thin air', R44 on the airline PA formula ('ladies and gentlemen, the captain has now turned on'), and R10 on the tech-support line ('have you tried unplugging it'). A rubric bank will read a recognized frame as 'coherent, well-formed setup' regardless of whether it earns anything.
proposals.upstream_parent: repeat-entrant exposure to stock caption templates circulating in the contest community

proposals.name: Homophone or polysemy pivot words
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption contains a word or short phrase that carries two available readings at once (a homophone, homograph, or a term with a literal and an idiomatic sense both live in context). 0 = every word has one operative reading; 4 = a mildly ambiguous term that could be read two ways; 7 = one clear double-meaning term functioning as the caption's pivot; 10 = two or more double-meaning terms, or a single pivot whose two readings are both explicitly supported by the surrounding words. Score the presence and load-bearing role of the ambiguity only. Do not judge whether the wordplay lands, whether it is groan-worthy or delightful, whether it is original, or whether the caption is good.
proposals.rationale: Pun machinery is mechanically detectable and is very likely an explicit criterion in the bank, so it accrues scorecard credit whether or not it produces anything. The slice is dense with pivots on the scorecard-high side: R25 ('spare ribs'), R27 ('roaming charges'), R45 ('a fixture at this spot'), R26 ('illegal aliens'), R60 ('i don't trust the poles'), R53 ('what shape you're in'). Tagged mixed because pun construction is also a real craft skill, so the discount should be reported as a band, not silently applied.

proposals.name: Pre-1990 cultural referents and explicit age self-reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption draws on cultural material, products, or life-stage framing that indexes an older cohort. Count: brands, snacks, media, or music that were prominent before roughly 1990; institutions or rituals of an earlier era; explicit self-description as old, middle-aged, obsolete, or outmoded; long-marriage or grown-children domestic framing. 0 = no cohort-indexing material; 5 = one such referent; 10 = two or more, or a referent that the whole caption turns on. Score the presence of cohort-indexing material only. Do not infer or state anything about who wrote the caption, and do not judge whether the reference is dated, warm, tired, or good.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: the age of the person entering shapes the reference pool they reach for, and cohort is not merit. The fingerprint is the reference pool itself: R08 reaches for 'cracker jack', R11 for 'stairway to heaven', R19 asks 'does this make me look middle aged', R07 says 'we're dinosaurs, ronny', R56 frames around a long-married spouse. These are legible in text alone, so a text-only scorer can pick up the cohort effect; the channel exists to strip it out.

proposals.name: Vocative first names and named-addressee direct address
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption addresses a specific interlocutor by name or by an explicit relational vocative. 0 = no address term at all; 4 = a generic plural or role vocative ('guys', 'folks', 'ladies and gentlemen', 'sir'); 7 = a personal given name or a kinship vocative ('son', 'honey', 'dad') set off in the utterance; 10 = a named addressee plus a second address term, or a name placed as the caption's rhythmic hinge. Score the presence and prominence of the address term only. Do not judge whether the name is well chosen, whether it adds character or texture, and do not judge the caption's quality.
proposals.rationale: Upstream factor: submitters who have read many published captions learn that a dropped-in first name is a house mannerism and insert one to sound published; that is style mimicry, not comic substance. The fingerprint is the vocative: R07 ('we're dinosaurs, ronny'), R57 ('all you want, randy'), R24 ('student of the year is fine, son'), R11 ('stairway to heaven, guys'), R44 ('ladies and gentlemen'). Tagged mixed because a practiced entrant may also genuinely write better, so the parent plausibly causes real quality as well as the mannerism.
proposals.upstream_parent: veteran-entrant imitation of the venue's published-caption house style

proposals.name: Deadpan delivery of an absurd or charged statement
proposals.instruction: Score how flatly and matter-of-factly the caption states something absurd, alarming, or emotionally loaded, with no exclamation points, intensifiers, or other markers of surprise. A 10 is a caption that delivers a wildly incongruous fact or request in plain, unemotional, everyday phrasing. A 0 is a caption that is not incongruous at all, or that telegraphs its own absurdity with theatrical emphasis, exclamation points, or words like 'wow'/'seriously'.
proposals.rationale: Explains dense-favored, scorecard-missed items like R32 ('can i get a discount? this fish is dead') and R44 ('it's only until we board the plane'), and R57/R58, all of which are flat, unremarkable-sounding lines whose comic force comes purely from tonal mismatch with the situation -- a quality a criterion bank scored on content alone would likely undercredit.

proposals.name: Setup-then-reversal twist ending
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the caption establishes one expectation in its opening clause(s) and then subverts or recontextualizes that expectation in its final clause or word, producing a genuine reversal. A 10 is a caption whose ending completely flips the meaning set up at the start. A 0 is a single flat statement with no internal setup/payoff structure.
proposals.rationale: Dense ranks R11 ('i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince'), R21 ('have you tried unplugging it and leaving it unplugged'), and R23 ('about three years. how long have you been here') very high while the scorecard ranks them near the bottom; each hinges on a late clause overturning the reading built by the earlier clause, a structural property a static rubric may not isolate.

proposals.name: Naturalistic spoken-dialogue rhythm
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption reads like an utterance an actual person would say aloud -- contractions, hedges ('i suppose', 'well'), natural pauses, or self-correcting phrasing -- versus how much it reads like composed written prose. A 10 sounds fully like transcribed speech. A 0 reads like a written sentence or slogan nobody would actually say out loud.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('no, i can't help you get out of it like always and no, you can't run it through the dishwasher') and R19 ('if this doesn't break our lease, i don't have any better ideas') both score very high with the dense model and very low with the scorecard; both have the loose, repetitive cadence of real speech rather than the tighter, more 'written' phrasing typical of the scorecard's favorites.

proposals.name: Economy: full scenario in very few words
proposals.instruction: Score how much complete, specific comic situation the caption implies while using very few words, with no filler. A 10 is an extremely short caption (roughly under 8 words) that still conjures a specific, vivid scenario. A 0 is a caption that needs many words/clauses to set up its joke, or that is short but conveys nothing specific.
proposals.rationale: R18 ('did i miss anything') and R55 ('did we forget anything') are both four-word captions the dense model ranks near the top (dense_pct .907 and .868) while the scorecard ranks them near the bottom (.132 and .101); a criterion bank scoring explicit joke content would have little to reward in such short lines.

proposals.name: Entire caption phrased as a pointed question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the whole caption is delivered as a single sharp, loaded question directed at the listener, where the question itself (not a subsequent statement) carries the joke. A 10 is a caption consisting entirely of one such question. A 0 has no question, or a question that is incidental to where the joke actually lives.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('does this make me look middle aged'), R18 ('did i miss anything'), R55 ('did we forget anything'), and R56 ('do you have any idea who you're talking to') are all dense-favored, scorecard-disfavored, and all are single rhetorical questions -- suggesting the dense model rewards this compact interrogative form more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Status or power-dynamic reversal between speaker and addressee
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption reveals or implies an unexpected flip in relative status, authority, or seniority between speaker and addressee (an apparent subordinate turns out to be in charge, or vice versa). A 10 is a caption whose entire joke is this status reversal. A 0 implies no hierarchy or status relationship at all.
proposals.rationale: R38 ('ignore him. you now report directly to me') and R56 ('do you have any idea who you're talking to') are both dense-high/card-low and both work by flipping who holds power in the exchange; R23's veteran-newcomer reversal fits the same pattern.

proposals.name: Self-aware or existential meta-commentary by the speaker
proposals.instruction: Score whether the speaker is wryly commenting on their own nature, identity, role, or limitation, rather than describing external events or other people. A 10 is a caption built entirely around this kind of self-referential remark. A 0 is purely about external events with no self-commentary.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('at least i know i'm a puppet') and R53 ('what if i don't identify with either') are both strongly dense-favored (dense_pct .924 and .896) yet scorecard-disfavored (.040 and .148); both derive their humor from the speaker reflecting on their own condition rather than narrating a scene.

proposals.name: Brevity combined with dependence on the unseen image
proposals.instruction: Score the joint presence of (a) very short caption length and (b) clear dependence on an unseen visual detail to resolve the joke -- i.e., the caption alone is a deliberate fragment that implies it will click once paired with a specific image. A 10 is a very short caption that is obviously an incomplete visual punchline with a clear implied gap. A 0 is either long/self-contained or short but already fully sensible without any implied image.
proposals.rationale: R20 ('i think i'll mount this one on the ceiling') and R34 ('at least i know i'm a puppet') are dense-high/card-low; both are short lines that only cohere once you supply a specific unstated visual referent ('this one', the puppet strings), a composite property of length + image-reliance that a text-only rubric line item would struggle to capture.

proposals.name: Explicit, plainly-stated pun mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score how plainly and completely the caption spells out its wordplay or double meaning, such that the pun's mechanism is stated outright in the sentence rather than left for the reader to infer. A 10 is a caption where the double meaning is explicitly named or unpacked. A 0 has no wordplay, or wordplay so submerged that its mechanism is never stated.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('watch me pull out some hidden fees from thin air') and R42 ('is that chandelier going to keep getting bigger every time you tell this story') are both card-high/dense-low; both spell out their pun mechanism (magician/fees, Pinocchio-nose/chandelier) directly in the sentence, a fully-explained-joke quality the scorecard may be rewarding more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Reliance on a named public figure or current event
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption's humor depends on recognizing a specific named real-world public figure, politician, celebrity, or a recent/dated news event, such that the joke would not land for a reader unfamiliar with that reference. A 10 only makes sense with that specific topical knowledge. A 0 is fully self-contained and timeless, with no real-world named references.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('if trump wins again'), R41 ('they've come back for marjorie taylor greene'), and R48 ('perhaps elon musk does have too much money') are all card-high/dense-low; all require recognizing a specific real, currently-topical public figure, a dependency the scorecard appears to reward that the dense model does not.

proposals.name: Direct address of a named individual by first name
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption directly addresses a specific person by a personal first name (a fictional/generic name used as if speaking to a particular character in the scene, not a public figure). A 10 is a caption built around naming the addressee by first name as part of its delivery. A 0 has no named addressee at all.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('you can advocate for wind power all you want, randy...') and R50 ('we're dinosaurs, ronny... we don't do whimsy') are both card-high/dense-low and both use a first-name direct address as a structural device, distinct from reliance on real public figures (A10).

proposals.name: List or parallel-clause enumeration structure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption's joke is built by listing multiple items or stringing together multiple parallel clauses/phrases (e.g., 'X, Y, and Z') rather than a single simple clause. A 10 is explicitly structured as a list or clear multi-item enumeration the joke depends on. A 0 is a single simple clause with no listing or parallel structure.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('i'd like to order four hot dogs, 2 boxes of cracker jack and 2 sheets of drywall') and R24 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') are both card-high/dense-low and both build their punchline through an explicit list or parallel two-clause construction.

proposals.name: Stacked / compound double meanings
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption contains two or more distinct double meanings or puns operating simultaneously, as opposed to a single pun. A 10 has at least two independent, load-bearing wordplay mechanisms both present. A 0 has no wordplay, or exactly one single pun/double meaning.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('another job lost to illegal aliens', playing on both immigration anxiety and literal space aliens) and R60 ('stairway to heaven, guys, the short version', stacking a song reference with a literal-stairs meaning) are both card-high/dense-low and both layer more than one simultaneous reading into a short line.

proposals.name: Dark or morbid content in a mundane frame
proposals.instruction: Score how much the caption pairs genuinely dark, morbid, or serious subject matter (injury, death, loss, medical harm, financial desperation) with a cheerful, casual, or mundane tone that treats it lightly. A 10 delivers serious/dark content in a notably chipper or offhand register. A 0 has no dark content, or dark content delivered in a tone matching its seriousness.
proposals.rationale: R24 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') and R33 ('don't cry. now, daddy can get his full 1200 stimulus') are both card-high/dense-low and both juxtapose genuinely dark subject matter with a breezy, matter-of-fact delivery, a tonal-juxtaposition property distinct from the deadpan-register criterion (A01), which targets flatness rather than dark-content pairing specifically.

proposals.name: Explicit if-then conditional or ultimatum structure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the caption is built as an explicit 'if X, then Y' conditional, threat, or consequence statement, where the joke depends on that if-then logical structure. A 10 is a caption whose entire sentence is an explicit conditional/ultimatum. A 0 has no conditional structure at all.
proposals.rationale: R47 ('go and enjoy the lights if you must, but if you are not back by 11 30 you're sleeping on the screen door again') and R40 ('this pizza's on me if you never order from us again') are both card-high/dense-low and both hinge entirely on an explicit if-then consequence structure that the scorecard seems to reward more than the dense model does.

proposals.name: Named real-world proper-noun density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption text names specific real-world people, public figures, brands, or place names (proper nouns) rather than using only generic, unnamed references. 0 = no proper nouns of people/places/brands appear anywhere in the text; 10 = the caption's content is built entirely around one or more explicitly named real-world entities. Do not judge whether naming these entities makes the caption funnier or better as a contest entry -- score only how much explicit naming is present in the text.
proposals.rationale: Rows R06 ("marjorie taylor greene"), R10 ("trump"), and R26 ("elon musk") all name specific real people and sit in the dense_low_card_high slice, while rows like R20 and R39 use zero proper nouns and sit in dense_high_card_low -- named-entity density is a purely lexical, countable surface feature separate from any judgment of wit, though shared-recognition of a named figure could genuinely add resonance, so it is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: News-cycle / dated-event topicality anchor
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how strongly the caption text ties itself to a specific, datable real-world news event or policy moment (for example a pandemic-era reference to a stimulus payment or mask shortage, or an election-cycle reference) as opposed to describing a timeless, undated scenario. 0 = nothing in the text dates it to a specific news moment; 10 = the caption is unmistakably anchored to one identifiable real-world news event. Do not judge whether the topical reference is clever or well-executed -- score only how strongly the text is anchored to a specific datable event.
proposals.rationale: R01 ("full 1200 stimulus") and R15 ("easier to get than an n95 mask") both date themselves to the COVID-relief/pandemic news window and land in dense_low_card_high; if such items were selected partly for topical buzz at submission time rather than caption craft, timeliness is a nuisance, though genuine relatability from shared current events could also make a caption authentically funnier, so it is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing relative to news cycle / editorial recency bias

proposals.name: Named-addressee vocative persona marker
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption directly addresses a named individual by a personal first name inside the dialogue (a vocative, e.g. "Ronny", "Randy") as opposed to addressing no one by name. 0 = no personal name is used to address anyone in the text; 10 = the caption's dialogue is explicitly and centrally addressed to a named person. Do not judge whether naming the addressee is a good comedic choice -- score only how much a personal name is used as direct address.
proposals.rationale: R33 ("we're dinosaurs, ronny...") and R50 ("...you're not going to escape your fossil fuel destiny", addressed to "randy") both use a named vocative and sit in dense_low_card_high; this could reflect a recurring-persona habit of experienced repeat submitters rather than fit to this specific item, though sustained practice from repeat authorship could also genuinely improve craft, so it is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Extreme caption brevity / terseness
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how terse the caption is by word count alone: 0 = a long, multi-clause caption (roughly 18 or more words); 10 = an extremely short caption (5 words or fewer) with no subordinate or explanatory clause. Score strictly by word/clause count -- do not judge whether the caption's length is appropriate or effective.
proposals.rationale: R39 ("did we forget anything", 4 words) and R57 ("did i miss anything", 4 words) are both extremely terse and sit in dense_high_card_low, versus much longer items like R56 (21 words) and R52 (21 words); terseness could signal a submitter's learned knowledge of what gets selected rather than intrinsic quality, though real economy of language is also a genuine comedic virtue, so it is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's insider knowledge of editorial brevity norms (repeat-entrant savvy)

proposals.name: Two-clause setup/twist scaffolding (recycled-joke shape)
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption follows an explicit two-part "setup, then twist/contrast" sentence structure -- for example clauses joined by "but", an if/then construction, or a comma-linked concession followed by a reversal -- of the kind common in generic stand-alone jokes, as opposed to a single unstructured utterance. 0 = a single clause/utterance with no setup-twist connective; 10 = a clearly two-part sentence with an explicit setup clause and a contrasting payoff clause joined by a connective. Do not judge whether the joke structure lands well -- score only how much this two-part connective structure is present.
proposals.rationale: R50 ("you can advocate for wind power all you want, randy, but you're not going to escape your fossil fuel destiny") and R42 ("my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg") both show a generic setup-then-reversal shape that could be lifted or adapted from non-cartoon joke material rather than built for this specific image, which would be a pure nuisance rather than a source of genuine tailored quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: caption reuse / adaptation from non-cartoon-specific comedy material

proposals.name: Specific numeric quantity citation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption includes one or more explicit numbers or counted quantities (a dollar figure, a count of items, a time span given in numerals or number-words) as opposed to using no numbers at all. 0 = no numbers or quantities appear anywhere; 10 = the caption's content is built around one or more explicit numeric quantities. Do not judge whether the specific number chosen is funny or apt -- score only how much explicit numeric quantity is present.
proposals.rationale: R01 ("1200 stimulus"), R54 ("four hot dogs, 2 boxes of cracker jack and 2 sheets of drywall"), and R42 ("45 pounds") all foreground explicit numerals and sit in dense_low_card_high; digits stand out visually when many text captions are skimmed together, which is a pure attention artifact unrelated to whether the caption is actually funny.
proposals.upstream_parent: numeric-caption visual salience during editorial skim / vote tallying

proposals.name: Ellipsis/dash pause-timing punctuation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses an ellipsis ("...") or an em/en-dash ("--" or "-") as a mid-sentence pause or delivery-timing marker, as opposed to using only standard sentence punctuation (periods, commas, question marks). 0 = no ellipsis or dash pause marker anywhere in the text; 10 = the caption's structure is built around one or more ellipsis/dash pauses. Do not judge whether the pause improves the caption's timing -- score only how much this punctuation device is present.
proposals.rationale: R32 ("...i'll be waiting for a princess... not a prince") and R10 ("it's the trump lure -- it works best with bottom feeders") both use an ellipsis or dash as a formatting habit; this is a pure typographic/layout marker independent of content, though such punctuation is also a recognized craft device for comedic timing, so it is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Specialist abbreviation / acronym shorthand
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses a technical, medical, or otherwise domain-specific abbreviation or acronym (for example a string of periods-separated initials, or specialist shorthand) as opposed to using only everyday plain-language words. 0 = no specialist abbreviation or acronym appears; 10 = the caption's key content depends on a specialist abbreviation or acronym. Do not judge whether the abbreviation is used cleverly -- score only how much specialist shorthand is present.
proposals.rationale: R08 ("my husband is an o.b.g.y.n") and R15 ("easier to get than an n95 mask") both hinge on a specialist abbreviation and sit in dense_low_card_high; this is a lexical/orthographic quirk (periods-in-initials formatting, domain jargon) rather than a quality judgment, though an acronym-as-reveal can also be genuine craft, so it is tagged mixed.

proposals.name: Bare fill-in-the-blank template fragment
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption reads as an extremely minimal, fixed-slot phrase template (for example a two-word menu announcement, a bare "X or Y" binary choice, or a short exclamatory fragment with no full sentence) as opposed to a fully formed original sentence. 0 = a complete, original sentence; 10 = a bare template fragment with almost no unique content beyond filling a slot. Do not judge whether the minimal template is effective -- score only how much the caption resembles a bare fill-in-the-blank fragment.
proposals.rationale: R22 ("chicken or rabbit") and R60 ("special tonight - spare ribs") are both reduced to a bare template with almost no elaboration and sit in dense_low_card_high; this format-level minimalism is a pure structural artifact rather than a marker of crafted wit.

proposals.name: First-person deadpan confessional statement form
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption is phrased as a flat, first-person confessional or self-descriptive statement centered on "I" (e.g. "I am not...", "I don't trust...", "I know I'm...") delivered without exclamation or elaboration, as opposed to being phrased as dialogue about someone/something else or as a question. 0 = no first-person confessional statement is present; 10 = the entire caption is a single flat first-person confessional statement. Do not judge whether the confessional voice is funny or distinctive -- score only how much this first-person deadpan statement form is present.
proposals.rationale: R04 ("to begin with, i am not anti-vacs"), R13 ("i don't trust the poles anymore"), and R40 ("at least i know i'm a puppet") all use this flat first-person confessional form and sit in dense_high_card_low; a single repeat submitter's honed voice could be over-represented across many entries independent of per-item fit, though sustained practice from repeat authorship could also genuinely raise craft, so it is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: authorial persona/style consistency across repeat submissions (single prolific author's voice bank)

proposals.name: Dual-reading depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording supports two coherent, mutually enriching readings; score 0 when it has only one straightforward meaning or an incoherent ambiguity.
proposals.rationale: R12 turns an idiom into an elevator situation, while R31 makes a communication metaphor physically literal; both reward layered interpretation.

proposals.name: Recontextualizing turn
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a final word or clause sharply changes how the setup is understood; score 0 when the ending merely adds information or states the obvious.
proposals.rationale: R10 pivots from a generic princess expectation to a romantic demand, and R21 transforms academic praise into a dog-show comparison.

proposals.name: Implied conversational premise
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like a natural reply that lets the reader reconstruct an unstated exchange; score 0 when it lacks a believable conversational situation.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R52 both imply a power-laden exchange through ordinary dialogue, while their humor depends on what preceded the line.

proposals.name: Compression efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every word efficiently builds a setup, attitude, or comic turn; score 0 when the wording is padded, redundant, or too compressed to establish a mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R29 achieve strong turns with very little language, suggesting value in dense semantic packaging rather than length alone.

proposals.name: Concrete absurd escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise escalates through a specific, disproportionate concrete detail; score 0 when details are random, merely descriptive, or non-escalatory.
proposals.rationale: R03 escalates a food order with drywall, and R42 escalates a practical request into an elaborate dishwasher solution.

proposals.name: Role/status inversion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption unexpectedly reverses who has authority, agency, or control; score 0 when relationships remain entirely conventional.
proposals.rationale: R34 reveals the speaker as a puppet, while R52 abruptly makes the speaker the listener’s superior.

proposals.name: Deadpan tonal control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when extraordinary circumstances are delivered with restrained, matter-of-fact confidence; score 0 when the line overexplains, strains for laughter, or uses a mismatched tone.
proposals.rationale: R11 treats overthinking as something to avoid, and R29 calmly celebrates an unexplained solution; both depend on understated delivery.

proposals.name: Idiom literalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom or expression is converted into a vivid literal situation without losing its original association; score 0 when the phrase is used conventionally or the literal reading is forced.
proposals.rationale: R01 literalizes mounting something on the ceiling, and R12 physically realizes an elephant-in-the-room expression in an elevator.

proposals.name: Visualizable physical staging
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording implies a clear, comic arrangement of bodies, objects, or movement; score 0 when no concrete staging can be inferred from the text.
proposals.rationale: R01 supplies a memorable ceiling arrangement, while R48 specifies coordinated action involving a tablecloth and several participants.

proposals.name: Distinctive speaker voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line clearly reveals a particular personality, relationship, or social role; score 0 when it could be spoken by anyone without changing the joke.
proposals.rationale: R07 establishes a recognizable parental or partner-like complaint about a nocturnal creature, and R51 strongly defines an authoritarian household voice.

proposals.name: Topical reference integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a public figure, event, or issue is essential to the joke’s mechanism and is transformed by the wording; score 0 when the reference is detachable name-dropping or a generic opinion.
proposals.rationale: R16 turns Trump into bait for bottom feeders, whereas R24 and R38 mainly invoke public figures without developing an equally specific comic mechanism.

proposals.name: Payoff-bearing specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when numbers, objects, names, or technical details materially sharpen the comic premise; score 0 when specificity is decorative, interchangeable, or cluttering.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses time and biological details to define the situation, while R45 uses instrument names to make the proposed exchange precise and surprising.

proposals.name: Freshness beyond stock jokes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption combines familiar material in an unusually specific angle or formulation; score 0 when it reproduces a predictable pun, cliché, or standard one-liner template.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R05 rely on highly familiar wordplay patterns, illustrating how surface cleverness can be mistaken for originality.

proposals.name: Shock transformed into insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sensitive or harsh premise produces a precise reversal or observation beyond mere shock; score 0 when harm, stereotype, or offensiveness is the entire comic device.
proposals.rationale: R26 and R33 use bodily loss or a hostile stereotype as the main payload, so this criterion distinguishes substantive transformation from shock alone.

proposals.name: Spoken timing and cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when pauses, repetition, lists, counts, or sentence rhythm create unmistakable performance timing; score 0 when the line is flat, awkward, or rhythmically inert.
proposals.rationale: R42 uses repeated refusals for buildup, while R48 and R60 use coordinated counting to create an audible comic beat.

proposals.name: Numeric specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of digits, counts, prices, measurements, ages, or exact quantities; judge only presence, never whether this specificity is good.
proposals.rationale: Exact quantities appear in R01, R05, R08, R23, R35, R36, and R40. They may attract pattern-based attention or normalization artifacts without indicating contest-entry quality.

proposals.name: Temporal anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of clock times, dates, durations, deadlines, recurrence, or time-of-day wording; judge only presence, never whether the timing reference is good.
proposals.rationale: Temporal traces occur in R05, R07, R14, R35, and R40. Submission timing or deadline pressure could produce such wording and affect reception, while also plausibly affecting time available for genuine crafting.

proposals.name: Named-entity salience
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of recognizable people, places, brands, media outlets, or institutions being named; judge only presence, never whether the reference is good.
proposals.rationale: R28 names Venice, R37 names Fox News, R42 names Marjorie Taylor Greene, and R47 names Elon Musk. Familiar entities can trigger recognition independently of caption quality, though choosing an accessible reference can also genuinely help an entry.

proposals.name: Current-affairs anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption invokes recent public controversies, policies, crises, or partisan issues; judge only presence, never whether the topical reference is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 invokes stimulus payments, R15 N95 masks, R27 fossil-fuel politics, R43 Trump, and R60 immigration. News-cycle exposure can make text conspicuous independently of quality, while topical relevance may also genuinely improve a caption.

proposals.name: Professional jargon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of medical, legal, financial, bureaucratic, or workplace-specific terminology; judge only presence, never whether the terminology is good.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses medical terminology, R21 financial language, R30 legal language, R45 corporate language, and R55 telecom terminology. Domain vocabulary can signal expertise or trigger reader familiarity without proving entry quality, though expertise may also support better writing.

proposals.name: Caption length
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of word count, clause count, and elaboration relative to a short one-line caption; judge only textual length, never whether being longer is good.
proposals.rationale: R04, R16, R23, and R40 are highly elaborated, while R06, R10, and R50 are very compressed. Length can affect attention and model representation independently of how good the joke is.

proposals.name: Copyediting signals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of standardized spelling, apostrophes, punctuation, sentence boundaries, and deliberate typographic marks; judge only visible editing signals, never whether the text is well written.
proposals.rationale: R04, R09, R27, R43, and R57 display comparatively deliberate syntax or punctuation. Editorial assistance can create a detectable polish signal independent of contest quality, while editing may also genuinely improve an entry.

proposals.name: Authority hierarchy
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit rank, command, selection, family hierarchy, deference, or reporting relationships; judge only presence, never whether the authority framing is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 uses daddy, R11 uses son, R45 describes downsizing selection, R51 uses direct reporting, and R59 invokes a captain. Status language may cue social authority independently of quality, though a distinctive authority perspective can also contribute to genuine humor.

proposals.name: Borrowed phrase markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of recognizable titles, slogans, idioms, stock lines, or adapted catchphrases; judge only resemblance or allusion, never whether the borrowing is good.
proposals.rationale: R16 uses the elephant in the room idiom, R19 references Stairway to Heaven, R49 echoes a familiar troubleshooting line, and R59 uses an applause-sign premise. Template familiarity can prompt recognition without indicating quality, although adaptation can sometimes genuinely help.
proposals.upstream_parent: professional assistance or prior exposure to cultural templates

proposals.name: Conversational scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of formulaic dialogue openings or frames such as questions, refusals, guesses, imperatives, or routine replies; judge only presence, never whether the framing is good.
proposals.rationale: Routine scaffolds appear in R03, R06, R10, R21, R31, R41, R49, and R50. Such frames may be overrepresented because they resemble common caption templates, creating a text-pattern effect unrelated to entry quality.

proposals.name: Implied Premise Clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption assumes an unstated situation but gives enough cues to reconstruct it; score 0 when its context is opaque or absent.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high lines such as R01, R08, R11, and R26 rely on compact, recoverable premises rather than explicit exposition.

proposals.name: Natural Spoken Cadence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the line sounds like spontaneous, believable speech with natural rhythm; score 0 when it reads like a slogan, label, or assembled joke fragment.
proposals.rationale: R02, R06, R07, and R17 have conversational phrasing, unlike more formulaic lines such as R25 and R49.

proposals.name: Deadpan Underreaction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when bizarre or high-stakes circumstances are treated with calm, matter-of-fact language; score 0 when the tone merely matches the event or announces the joke.
proposals.rationale: R06, R18, R20, and R60 derive force from understated responses to extreme situations.

proposals.name: Consequence Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when successive clauses or actions raise the risk, commitment, or absurdity to a sharper endpoint; score 0 when the line has no progression.
proposals.rationale: R06, R29, R36, and R60 build toward increasingly consequential actions or implications.

proposals.name: Revealing Character Voice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when wording distinctly reveals the speaker’s status, attitude, identity, or relationship; score 0 when any anonymous speaker could say it unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R14, R17, R37, and R57 communicate strong speaker positions through voice rather than exposition.

proposals.name: Verbal Compression
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every phrase efficiently advances the premise or punchline and nothing feels expendable; score 0 when the wording is padded, repetitive, or incomplete.
proposals.rationale: R02, R08, R11, and R58 achieve substantial comic implication in very few words.

proposals.name: Semantic Hinge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a word or phrase supports two coherent readings and the line pivots between them; score 0 when wording has only one literal meaning or is merely ambiguous.
proposals.rationale: R03, R25, R31, R38, and R49 use words whose alternate meanings create the central turn.

proposals.name: Grand-to-Mundane Deflation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a lofty, dramatic, or philosophical frame is undercut by a precisely banal detail; score 0 when no contrast in scale or register exists.
proposals.rationale: R03, R23, R42, and R56 juxtapose grand framing with ordinary procedural or status details.

proposals.name: Purposeful Exact Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when numbers, quantities, or concrete details sharpen the premise and feel indispensable; score 0 when specificity is arbitrary decoration.
proposals.rationale: R04, R24, R28, and R55 use exact quantities or timing to intensify the imagined situation.

proposals.name: Topical Transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a political, cultural, or current reference is transformed into the joke’s mechanism; score 0 when it is only a recognizable name, issue, or slogan.
proposals.rationale: R05, R10, R35, R48, and R53 show how topical references can either drive or merely furnish a premise.

proposals.name: Coherent Category Collision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when seemingly unrelated domains are joined by an understandable, surprising relationship; score 0 when the juxtaposition is random or disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R04, R24, R51, and R56 connect bodily, commercial, professional, and evaluative categories in unexpected ways.

proposals.name: Concrete Visual Action
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording suggests an immediately stageable physical action or prop interaction; score 0 when it remains purely abstract or declarative.
proposals.rationale: R02, R19, R29, R36, R46, and R58 provide clear physical actions that can animate a cartoon scene.

proposals.name: Fresh Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar situation or phrase is given an unexpected but coherent angle; score 0 when it states an obvious observation or stock association.
proposals.rationale: R07, R15, R21, and R45 reframe recognizable situations, while their compactness makes the freshness easy to miss with checklist-style evaluation.

proposals.name: Scene-Conscious Meta-Awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the caption exploits conventions of conversation, performance, storytelling, or cartoon presentation itself; score 0 when it treats the situation without self-awareness.
proposals.rationale: R21, R22, R33, R42, and R60 explicitly play with applause, games, stories, social scenes, or the phrase “in the room.”

proposals.name: Late-Line Pivot
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the key reinterpretation or comic reveal arrives at the final phrase after a credible setup; score 0 when the line is flat throughout or reveals its premise immediately.
proposals.rationale: R06, R14, R20, R36, and R60 reserve their sharpest change in meaning for the ending.

proposals.name: Interrogative framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much is the caption phrased as a question through interrogative syntax or question wording? Judge only extent, not whether the question is good, funny, or effective.
proposals.rationale: Question framing is a visible grammatical habit that a text model can associate with contest performance without measuring caption quality. Examples include R01 and R03, with similar forms in R05 and R56.

proposals.name: Stock conversational templates
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use familiar conversational templates such as “i guess,” “what if,” “have you tried,” or “did we”? Judge only the amount of formulaic wording, not whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: Reusable dialogue templates may act as corpus-style markers while saying little about intrinsic quality. They appear in R04, R05, R15, R35, and R44.

proposals.name: Current-event anchoring
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption explicitly invoke contemporary political, public-health, technology, or economic events? Judge only topical presence, not whether the reference improves the caption.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can leave a textual trace through references to the news cycle, and timing may also influence which topics an author develops. Examples include R24 and R43, alongside R40 and R53.

proposals.name: Quantified specificity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain exact numbers, measurements, times, counts, or quantified lists? Judge only numerical detail, not whether the detail is useful or amusing.
proposals.rationale: Numerical density is an easily learned textual proxy independent of caption quality. It is visible in R20, R33, R50, R51, and R59.

proposals.name: Formatting irregularity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain nonstandard spelling, contractions, spacing, punctuation, or numeral formatting? Judge only visible irregularity, not whether it is intentional or good.
proposals.rationale: Interface normalization or hurried copying can create artifacts that a model mistakes for author or venue signals. Examples include “anti-vacs” in R09, “11 30” in R20, and “its” in R52.

proposals.name: Specialized jargon
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use occupational, legal, commercial, technical, or institutional vocabulary? Judge only the amount of domain-specific language, not whether it is apt or sophisticated.
proposals.rationale: Professional background can affect both available subject matter and genuine writing ability, making this a potentially mixed nuisance. Specialized terms appear in R02, R18, R36, R46, and R47.
proposals.upstream_parent: author professional background or institutional resources

proposals.name: Cultural allusion density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption rely on recognizable entertainment, cultural, or genre allusions? Judge only the presence and extent of allusion, not whether the reference works.
proposals.rationale: Cultural exposure may leave recognizable references in the text and may also provide material for genuinely strong captions. Examples include “best in show” in R08, “Stairway to Heaven” in R45, and the airline announcement convention in R48.

proposals.name: Status positioning
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption contain explicit claims or cues about authority, hierarchy, prestige, rank, or social standing? Judge only status language, not whether the stance is convincing or funny.
proposals.rationale: Author seniority or social position may influence both wording and actual craft, so the channel is plausibly mixed. Status cues occur in R08, R18, R37, and R56.

proposals.name: Editorial elaboration
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption show visibly elaborated syntax, multiple linked clauses, explicit temporal or conditional relations, and carefully maintained referents? Judge only textual elaboration, not writing quality.
proposals.rationale: Editing assistance can leave structural fingerprints and can also improve genuine caption quality, making this a sensitivity channel. Elaborated constructions appear in R20, R27, and R55.

proposals.name: Life-stage and family markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption explicitly mention age, family roles, parent-child relations, marriage, or domestic life context? Judge only the amount of biographical or family-role material, not whether it creates a good caption.
proposals.rationale: Demographic and life-context factors can shape textual subject matter and may also influence authentic perspective, so the channel is mixed. Examples include “middle aged” in R12, family roles in R33, and “daddy” in R59.
